analogy.p: A photocopy has exactly the same writing as the original, just like a clone has exactly the same genes as the parent. Tissue culture and cuttings are like photocopying a page over and over, so you get many identical pages quickly. Adult cell cloning is like taking the text of one document (the nucleus) and printing it onto a blank sheet (the egg with its nucleus removed). The analogy breaks down because a photocopy is a flat, exact copy, whereas a clone is a living organism whose features also depend on its environment as it grows, so clones can look slightly different. Also, a page of photocopies has no risk of dying out together, but a population of identical organisms can all be wiped out by one disease
analogy.t: Cloning is like photocopying a document

bullets: **Clone** = a genetically identical copy. Cells from mitosis are genetically identical to the parent cell.
**Asexual reproduction** involves only **one parent**, no gametes and no fertilisation, so there is **no genetic variation** in the offspring.
**Sexual reproduction** (two gametes, meiosis, fertilisation) mixes the genes from two parents so offspring are all different. Cloning avoids this.
Identical twins are natural clones: one embryo splits in two early on, and each part grows into a person with the same genes.
The four spec methods: **tissue culture, cuttings** (plants); **embryo transplants, adult cell cloning** (animals).
Clones can differ in appearance a little because of **environmental differences** such as diet, light, soil or upbringing.
This is biology (triple) only: it is not in the Combined Science specification.
core.h: What a clone is and why clones are identical
core.p: A **clone** is an organism that is **genetically identical** to its parent, or to another organism, because it was produced without the mixing of genes that happens in sexual reproduction. Natural clones are made by **asexual reproduction**, where a single parent divides by **mitosis**, and mitosis copies the DNA exactly. The four cloning techniques in the specification are artificial ways of making clones on purpose. Because clones have the **same alleles**, any difference between them is caused by their environment, not their genes. That is why clones are useful for scientists and farmers who want a reliable, predictable organism.

bullets: **Preserving rare plant species**: tissue culture can produce many plants from a tiny sample of an endangered plant.
**Commercial use in nurseries**: thousands of identical plants (for example orchids or crops) can be grown quickly all year.
**Gardeners** use cuttings to copy a favourite plant for free.
**Farming**: embryo transplants spread the genes of the best cow or sheep to many offspring, for example for high milk yield or good meat.
**Research**: identical organisms give a controlled variable (same genes) when testing drugs.
Plants can be produced **disease free** (tissue culture uses tiny pieces of plant tissue that may not carry disease) and in a **smaller space**, in a lab.
Clones guarantee **the same characteristics**, which is the key difference to selective breeding or sexual reproduction.
core.p: People clone organisms to make **many copies of one with a valuable characteristic**, to **preserve rare species**, and to produce plants quickly and cheaply. Sexual reproduction would shuffle the genes and could lose the desired trait, but a clone is guaranteed to have it. Cloning is used in horticulture (nurseries and gardens), farming (high-yielding or high-quality animals) and conservation. It also supports research, because identical organisms make **fair tests** when comparing treatments.

bullets: Definition: using **small groups of cells** from part of a plant to grow **identical new plants**.
Cells are grown on **sterile agar** with **nutrients and hormones**. Hormones tell the cells to develop into roots and shoots (extension detail).
Plant cells are **unspecialised or can become unspecialised**, so a small piece can grow into a whole plant.
**Aseptic technique** (sterile equipment, gloves, clean workspace) prevents bacteria and fungi from contaminating the culture.
Advantages: can produce **very large numbers** quickly, in a **small space**, **all year round**, from tiny samples; plants are identical and can be **disease free**.
Used for **rare plants** (e.g. orchids) and commercially in nurseries for crops and house plants.
Disadvantages: needs **specialist equipment and skill**, is **more expensive** than cuttings, and all plants are genetically identical (risk).
Link: required practical on growing microorganisms uses the same aseptic ideas (agar, sterile conditions).
core.p: **Tissue culture** is **using small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants**. The cells are placed on a sterile **nutrient medium, usually agar**, containing **mineral nutrients and plant hormones (growth regulators)**, and kept warm and in the light. The cells divide by mitosis to form a mass of cells, then plantlets with roots and shoots appear, which are moved to compost. The method is important for **preserving rare plant species** and for **commercial use in nurseries**. Everything has to be kept **sterile (aseptic)** because microorganisms grow rapidly on nutrient agar and would kill the plant cells.

bullets: **Older, simple** technique used by **gardeners** and nurseries.
A cut piece of **stem** from the parent is planted in **compost** (or water) and kept moist.
**Rooting powder** (auxin hormone) speeds up root growth (extension detail).
Produces **many identical plants** from one parent, without needing seeds.
Advantages: **cheap**, no special equipment, quick to learn, new plants have the **same features** (flower colour, taste) as the parent.
Disadvantages: a limited number of plants from one parent; any **disease** in the parent passes to the clones; **not all cuttings root**.
Not all plants grow from cuttings easily.
Compare with tissue culture: cuttings = cheap and low-tech but fewer plants; tissue culture = lab-based, many plants, can be disease free.
core.p: **Cuttings** are an **older, simple method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant**. A piece of stem (often with a few leaves) is cut from the parent plant, the lower leaves are removed, and the stem is planted in moist compost, often after being dipped in **rooting powder**, which contains **plant hormones (auxins)**. The cutting grows roots and develops into a new plant that is a **clone** of the parent. It is cheap and simple but produces fewer plants than tissue culture and carries any disease in the parent.

bullets: Start with an embryo from **sexual reproduction** (egg + sperm), so it has genes from **both parents**.
At an early stage the cells are **not yet specialised** (each can still become any cell type), so they can be **split apart**.
Each separated cell or group develops into a separate **identical embryo**.
The embryos are **transplanted into host mothers** to develop.
Result: several offspring that are **genetically identical to each other**, but **not to their parents**.
If cells were split after they had **specialised** the method would not work, because specialised cells cannot make a whole organism (exam favourite).
Use: farmers produce many animals with desirable characteristics from one high-quality pair.
Disadvantages: costly, needs specialist skill, may fail, **reduces genetic variation** in the herd.
core.p: **Embryo transplants** are a way of cloning **animals**. The cells of a **developing animal embryo are split apart before they become specialised**, so each cell can grow into a complete embryo. The identical embryos are then **transplanted into host mothers** (surrogates) where they develop normally. The calves or lambs that are born are **clones of each other**, but they are **not clones of either parent**, because the embryo was made by sexual reproduction (an egg fertilised by sperm). This technique is used in farming to produce many offspring from the best cow or bull.

bullets: Step 1: **remove the nucleus** from an **unfertilised egg cell** (so the egg has no genes of its own).
Step 2: take the **nucleus from an adult body cell** (e.g. skin cell) and **insert it** into the empty egg cell.
Step 3: an **electric shock** stimulates the egg to start **dividing by mitosis** to form an **embryo**.
Step 4: the embryo cells contain the **same genetic information as the adult** whose cell supplied the nucleus.
Step 5: at the **ball of cells** stage the embryo is **inserted into the womb of an adult female** (surrogate) to develop.
The baby is a clone of the **nucleus donor**, not of the egg donor or surrogate. (Mitochondria in the egg cytoplasm are from the egg donor, but nuclear genes are from the adult cell.)
Why remove the nucleus? So the new individual only has the **donor's DNA**, otherwise it would not be a clone.
Why an unfertilised egg? It is ready to develop into an embryo once it gets a full set of chromosomes and is stimulated.
Famous example: **Dolly the sheep** (1996), the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. She was put down at about six years old after developing lung disease.
core.h: Method 4: adult cell cloning (step by step)
core.p: **Adult cell cloning** makes an animal that is genetically identical to an **adult donor**. The steps must be in order: (1) the **nucleus is removed** from an **unfertilised egg cell**; (2) the **nucleus from an adult body cell**, for example a skin cell, is **inserted into the egg cell**; (3) an **electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide** to form an embryo; (4) these embryo cells contain the **same genetic information as the adult skin cell**; (5) when the embryo has developed into a **ball of cells**, it is **inserted into the womb of an adult female** to continue its development. The animal born is a clone of the animal that donated the nucleus.

bullets: **Tissue culture**: plants; small groups of cells; agar + nutrients + hormones; rare plants and nurseries.
**Cuttings**: plants; piece of stem; compost; older, simple, gardeners.
**Embryo transplant**: animals; embryo cells split apart before specialisation; implanted in host mothers; clones of each other not parents.
**Adult cell cloning**: animals; nucleus from adult body cell into egg without nucleus; electric shock; embryo implanted in womb; clone of the adult.
Plants vs animals: plants can be cloned from **many types of cell**; most animal cells are specialised, so the **egg cell environment** is needed to reprogramme the nucleus.
Only adult cell cloning produces a clone of an **existing adult**; embryo transplants produce clones of an **embryo**.
Each requires careful control of conditions, and has a failure rate.
core.p: Examiners like comparison tables, so you need to know the **organisms, the cells used and the main idea** of each method. Plant methods (tissue culture and cuttings) are easier because many plant cells can grow into whole plants. Animal methods are harder and have a low success rate. Understanding the pattern also helps you answer 'explain why' questions: plants clone easily because they keep **unspecialised cells** (meristem) while most animal cells specialise and lose that ability, which is why the nucleus from a specialised cell is placed in an egg.

bullets: **Preserve endangered species**: rare plants can be mass produced by tissue culture; animal cloning might help save species that struggle to breed.
**Predictable quality**: all clones have the same desirable characteristics (yield, taste, colour, disease resistance).
**Fast and large scale**: many plants or animals produced quickly from one parent.
**Cheap and simple** for plant cuttings.
**Research use**: genetically identical animals make **valid comparisons** when testing treatments.
Possible **medical uses** being researched (e.g. genetically matched tissues), but you should say 'could' as this is not established practice.
**Disease-free plants** from tissue culture can be grown for sale.
core.p: The advantages come from the fact that clones are **identical** and can be produced in large numbers. Farmers can be confident of getting the characteristics they want, conservationists can save species, and scientists get uniform organisms. In an evaluation you should link each advantage to a **consequence**, such as 'identical high-yielding plants, so a predictable harvest and more profit'. Think of the different groups affected: farmers, consumers, conservationists, scientists, and the animals themselves.

bullets: **Reduced genetic variation / gene pool**: all clones have the same alleles, so one disease could kill them all.
**Low success rate** in animal cloning: many embryos fail to develop or are lost, so it wastes eggs and time.
Some cloned animals have been born with **health problems** or have died young, which raises animal welfare concerns (evidence is limited).
**Expense**: needs skilled staff and specialist equipment.
**Ethical objections**: some people believe cloning animals, and especially humans, is wrong or 'playing God'; there are also religious views.
**Effect on farming**: smaller number of varieties may be grown, reducing biodiversity.
Cloning does not produce **new** characteristics; it only copies what already exists, so it cannot improve a species by itself.
Link to evolution: variation is needed for natural selection, so a population of clones cannot adapt to changing conditions.
core.p: Cloning has disadvantages that examiners expect you to know. The biggest scientific problem is **reduced genetic variation**: if all individuals are genetically identical, a single new disease or a change in the environment could wipe out the whole population, because none have a different allele that gives resistance. Adult cell cloning also has a **low success rate**, and some cloned animals have had **health problems**. There are also **ethical concerns**, particularly about cloning humans, and about animal welfare.

bullets: **Cloning**: asexual, identical offspring, no new genes, one parent (or one donor nucleus).
**Sexual reproduction**: two parents, gametes, variation.
**Selective breeding**: sexual reproduction with chosen parents, many generations, existing alleles.
**Genetic engineering**: new gene inserted from another organism, fast.
Cloning can be used **after** genetic engineering to produce many copies of a successful GM organism.
Embryo transplants use sexual reproduction first, then cloning of the embryo; the offspring are not clones of their parents.
Remember: only cloning gives genetically identical offspring.
core.h: Cloning compared with sexual reproduction, selective breeding and genetic engineering
core.p: The exam may ask you to compare these related ideas. In **sexual reproduction** two parents give variation. In **selective breeding** parents are chosen and bred over many generations. In **genetic engineering** a gene is moved from one organism to another. **Cloning** copies an organism exactly, and it can be combined with the others, for example by cloning a genetically engineered sheep so that the useful gene is passed on to all the clones.

bullets: Start: 'Cloning produces genetically identical organisms.'
Benefits (2 or more): preserve rare species, predictable quality, fast, cheap for cuttings, research.
Risks (2 or more): reduced variation so disease could kill all, low success rate, cost, ethical concerns, welfare.
Compare: plant cloning is cheap and low risk; animal cloning has more problems and objections.
Conclusion: a judgement such as 'plant cloning is beneficial but animal cloning raises ethical and scientific problems, so should be limited' with a **reason**.
Use the data: if given a table of success rates or costs, quote numbers.
Avoid vague words ('bad', 'unnatural'); say what the problem is.
core.h: Evaluating cloning: a structure for 6 mark answers
core.p: For a 6 mark 'evaluate' question you should write a balanced answer. Start with the context, then give advantages with consequences, then disadvantages with consequences, and end with a **justified conclusion**. Use paragraphs: benefits, risks, judgement. The best answers use specific names of techniques ('tissue culture preserves rare species') rather than generalising about 'cloning'. They also compare plants with animals, and show awareness that different people hold different views.

bullets: **Describe adult cell cloning (up to 5 marks)**: remove nucleus from egg; nucleus from adult body cell inserted; electric shock to divide; ball of cells; implanted into womb of female.
**Describe tissue culture (3 to 4 marks)**: small groups of cells; grown on sterile agar with nutrients and hormones; identical plants.
**Explain why clones are identical (2 marks)**: asexual/mitosis produces identical copies (1); same genetic information/alleles (1).
**State one risk (1 mark)**: reduced genetic variation, so a disease could kill all.
**Explain why embryos must be split early (2 marks)**: cells are not yet specialised, so each can develop into a whole organism.

**Compare clones from embryo transplants and adult cell cloning**: both give identical offspring; embryo transplant clones are identical to each other, not to the parents; adult cell clones are identical to the adult donor.
Make sure to use the words **genetically identical**, **nucleus**, **mitosis**, **embryo**, **host mother**.
core.h: Command words, marks and common exam questions
core.p: Know what each command word wants. **'Describe'** means set out the steps in order; for adult cell cloning the five steps earn up to 5 marks. **'Explain why'** needs a reason: e.g. 'the offspring are genetically identical because they come from one parent by mitosis'. **'Compare'** needs similarities and differences. **'Evaluate'** needs both sides and a conclusion. Typical questions: describe how cuttings are used; explain why tissue culture is used to preserve a rare plant; describe adult cell cloning; give one risk of cloning.

exam: **Learn adult cell cloning as a numbered 5-step list**: nucleus removed from egg; adult body cell nucleus inserted; electric shock; embryo (ball of cells); implanted in womb of an adult female.
**Describe** = steps in order, no reasons needed. **Explain** = add 'because'.
**1 mark**: one fact, e.g. 'tissue culture' or 'mitosis'.
**2 marks**: a statement plus a reason, e.g. 'the offspring are genetically identical because they are produced by mitosis'.
**4 marks**: usually the stages of a technique (tissue culture or embryo transplant); use the key words from the spec.
**6 marks**: evaluate cloning; two benefits, two risks, link each to a consequence, and conclude.
Always write **genetically identical**; avoid 'exact copy' without 'genes'.
Say **'before they become specialised'** for embryo transplants and 'host mother'.
Use **'reduced genetic variation'** and 'one disease could kill them all' for the main risk.
If asked to compare clones and offspring from sexual reproduction, use **comparative words** (more variation, whereas)
Percentage questions: percentage = part / whole x 100.

mistakes.r: Clones have identical genes; their appearance and characteristics can still be affected by the environment.
mistakes.w: Clones are exactly the same in every way.

mistakes.r: They are clones of each other (same embryo), but not of the parents, as they came from fertilisation.
mistakes.w: Embryo transplant offspring are clones of their parents.

mistakes.r: The nucleus is removed from the egg, and the nucleus from an adult body cell is inserted.
mistakes.w: In adult cell cloning the nucleus of the egg is used.

mistakes.r: No sperm; an electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide.
mistakes.w: A sperm cell is used to start the embryo.

mistakes.r: Cells must be split before they become specialised.
mistakes.w: The embryo is split once it has become specialised.

mistakes.r: It copies existing characteristics only; no new genes or variation.
mistakes.w: Cloning makes organisms with new characteristics.

mistakes.r: Both are asexual reproduction that makes clones by mitosis.
mistakes.w: Cuttings and tissue culture are sexual reproduction.

mistakes.r: The risk is reduced genetic variation, so a single disease could affect all the clones because they share the same alleles.
mistakes.w: The risk is that clones will get ill easily.

summary: Biology-only content: you must describe four ways of making **clones** (genetically identical organisms): tissue culture and cuttings in plants, and embryo transplants and adult cell cloning in animals, giving the steps of each and why they matter. You must also be able to weigh up the advantages and risks of cloning. It matters because it is a common 4 to 6 mark 'describe' or 'evaluate' question and links to mitosis, stem cells and genetic variation.

terms.d: A genetically identical copy of an organism or cell.
Reproduction involving only one parent, producing genetically identical offspring by mitosis, with no gametes or fertilisation.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
Using small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants.
An older, simple method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant.
Splitting apart cells from a developing animal embryo before they become specialised, then transplanting the identical embryos into host mothers.
Inserting the nucleus of an adult body cell into an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed, then stimulating it to form an embryo that is implanted into a female.
A female animal in whose womb a transplanted embryo develops (a surrogate).
A cell that has differentiated to carry out a particular function and (in animals) usually cannot become other cell types.
A female gamete that has not been fertilised and which contains half the chromosomes; used in adult cell cloning after its nucleus is removed.
The part of the cell that contains the genetic material (chromosomes).
A jelly containing nutrients on which microorganisms or plant cells are grown in the lab.
Working in a way that stops unwanted microorganisms contaminating cultures.
Differences in the alleles/genes between individuals of a species; clones have none.
All the alleles in a population; cloning reduces it.

worked.ans: Remove the nucleus from an unfertilised egg; insert the nucleus from an adult body cell; give an electric shock to make it divide into an embryo; when it is a ball of cells, implant it into the womb of an adult female sheep. The lamb is genetically identical to the adult that donated the nucleus.
worked.q: Describe how adult cell cloning can be used to produce a sheep that is genetically identical to an adult sheep. (5 marks)
steps: The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell (1).
A nucleus is taken from a body cell (e.g. skin cell) of the adult sheep and inserted into the egg cell (1).
An electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide (1) to form an embryo (1).
When the embryo is a ball of cells it is inserted into the womb of an adult female (1) where it develops.

worked.ans: 75%. The plants are produced by mitosis, which makes genetically identical cells, so they are clones of the parent with the same genes.
worked.q: A nursery takes 12 cuttings from one plant. 9 grow roots. Calculate the percentage that rooted, and explain why all the new plants are genetically identical. (3 marks)
steps: Cuttings are asexual reproduction, so each new plant grows by mitosis from the parent's cells.
Mitosis copies the DNA exactly, so all have the same alleles as the parent.

worked.ans: The calves are genetically identical because they all developed from cells of the same embryo. The risk is reduced genetic variation, so one disease could affect every animal in the herd.
worked.q: A scientist splits a cow embryo at the 8-cell stage into separate cells that are transplanted into host mothers. Explain why the calves are identical to each other, and one risk of using this method on a whole herd. (4 marks)
steps: The calves all came from the same embryo, which was formed from one egg and one sperm, so they have the same genes.
The cells were separated before specialisation, so each developed into a whole embryo.
Risk: the herd has no genetic variation.
A single disease could therefore kill all the cattle because none have resistant alleles.
